directions: Start indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost and transplant out after hardening off into well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; 3D African daisy flowers best in cool weather and can stall or go semi-dormant during peak summer heat. Uniquely textured, semi-double flowers combine a ring of flat, colorful outer petals with a raised, spoon-shaped or quilled inner row, giving each bloom a layered, three-dimensional effect quite different from the flat, single daisy form of standard osteospermum. Its compact, mounding habit and long bloom season in cool spring and fall weather make it a popular container and border plant, particularly valued in mild-winter climates where it can be treated as a short-lived perennial rather than a single-season annual. Deadhead spent flowers to prolong bloom, provide excellent drainage, and expect reduced flowering during the hottest, most humid weeks of summer.
sources: American Society for Horticultural Science reference

planting.note: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost and transplant out after danger of frost has passed into lean, well-drained soil in full sun; Kiss series gazania is bred for a compact, uniform habit and needs full sun to open its flowers fully.

directions: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost and transplant out after danger of frost has passed into lean, well-drained soil in full sun; Kiss series gazania is bred for a compact, uniform habit and needs full sun to open its flowers fully. Large, brightly colored, daisy-like flowers in shades of yellow, orange, pink, bronze, and white open wide over silvery, lobed foliage on a compact, uniform, well-branched plant bred for reliable garden performance and even flowering across the color range. Like other gazanias, the flowers close on cloudy days and at night, reopening each morning in bright sun, a heliotropic habit that makes them best appreciated in a sunny spot viewed during the day. Extremely heat- and drought-tolerant once established, it is well suited to a hot, dry border, rock garden, or container where richer, moisture-loving annuals would struggle, needing only occasional deep watering during extended dry spells.
sources: American Society for Horticultural Science reference

planting.note: Direct sow after last frost into average, well-drained soil in full sun; Cosmic Orange cosmos is a compact, early-flowering selection that tolerates heat, humidity, and poor soil better than most bedding annuals.

directions: Direct sow after last frost into average, well-drained soil in full sun; Cosmic Orange cosmos is a compact, early-flowering selection that tolerates heat, humidity, and poor soil better than most bedding annuals. Vivid, fully double to semi-double orange flowers cover a compact, bushy, finely textured plant that blooms earlier and stays notably shorter than standard sulfur cosmos, making it a good choice for the front of a border or a container where taller cosmos varieties would flop. Extremely heat- and drought-tolerant once established, it thrives in the same lean, poor soil and blazing summer sun that stresses many other bedding annuals, and it attracts butterflies and beneficial insects throughout its long bloom season. Deadhead spent flowers to prolong bloom, and expect reliable self-sowing in favorable conditions for volunteer plants the following year.

planting.note: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost and transplant out after danger of frost has passed into well-drained soil in full sun; QIS series globe amaranth is bred for long, straight cutting stems and uniform flower color across the series.

directions: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost and transplant out after danger of frost has passed into well-drained soil in full sun; QIS series globe amaranth is bred for long, straight cutting stems and uniform flower color across the series. Round, papery, clover-like flower heads in a full range of colors from white and pink to purple, orange, and carmine-red are held on long, straight, sturdy stems bred specifically for the cut-flower trade, holding their color and form for weeks as both fresh and dried arrangements. Extremely heat- and drought-tolerant once established, it thrives through the hottest, most humid part of summer when many other cut-flower annuals decline, blooming continuously from midsummer until frost with minimal deadheading needed. Harvest stems for drying just as flowers fully open, hanging bunches upside down in a dark, airy space to preserve their color for long-lasting dried arrangements.
sources: American Society for Horticultural Science reference
